old_title: Time and materials (T&M) or force account tickets

new.text: When extra work can't be priced in advance, it's usually done on time and materials (also called force account on public jobs). A good daily T&M ticket shows: date, project, change or work order number, and a clear description of the work and location (station); each worker's name, trade classification and hours (straight and overtime); each piece of equipment with ID, size, operating hours and standby hours; materials used with quantities (attach invoices); subcontractor and trucking costs; and the owner's representative's signature the same day. Pricing follows the contract: labor at actual wage plus burden, equipment at the contract's rate source (often the Rental Rate Blue Book or a state rate schedule), materials at invoice, plus the contract's markups. Photos before, during and after help. Unsigned or late tickets are the most common reason extra work goes unpaid. Your contract and project specs govern; this is general practice, not legal advice.
new.title: Time and materials (T&M) or force account tickets: what goes on the ticket for extra work
new.topic: Business, project management and job costing

old_title: Ductile iron pipe: push-on joint deflection table

new.text: Ductile iron push-on joints allow deflection at each joint. McWane Ductile's push-on joint chart (18 ft pipe length) lists: sizes 3 through 30 inch, maximum 5 degrees, maximum offset about 19 inches per 18 ft length, approximate curve radius 205 ft; 36 inch, 4 degrees, about 15 inches offset, radius about 260 ft. DIPRA's installation guide (Table 5, May 2015) lists 5 degrees for 3 to 12 inch and 3 degrees for 14 inch and larger push-on joints, noting larger pipe may allow more; without the maker's chart for 14 inch and up, use 3 degrees. Always use the specific maker's chart for the joint you have; mechanical joints and restrained joints have their own, often smaller, limits. Common design practice is to plan curves using less than the full allowable deflection (DIPRA guidance commonly suggests about 80% of maximum) so there's room for field adjustment. Assemble the joint straight and fully homed, then deflect.
new.title: Ductile iron pipe: push-on joint deflection table
new.source: McWane Ductile, push-on joint deflection chart

old_title: Quick reference: water main test numbers

new.text: Common water main numbers (check your spec, which governs). Hydrostatic test: AWWA C600 per U.S. Pipe, at least 1.25 times working pressure at the high point and 1.5 times at the low point; some utilities use 150 psi or 1.5 times working pressure, others working pressure plus 100 psi; hold at least 2 hours. Allowable make-up water L (gallons per hour) = S x D x square root of P / 148,000; for 1,000 ft of 8 inch at 150 psi, about 0.66 gal/hr. Disinfection (AWWA C651): continuous feed at least 25 mg/L, held 24 hours, at least 10 mg/L remaining; slug at least 100 mg/L for 3 hours; tablet about 25 mg/L for 24 hours. Bac-T samples every 1,200 ft plus end and branches, two consecutive acceptable sets. Flush before chlorinating at 3.0 ft per second or more (AWWA C651-14 Sec. 4.4.2; the 2005 edition said 2.5 ft per second, which is about 390 gpm in 8 inch). AWWA lists C651-23 as the current edition of the disinfection standard; the numbers here are from the 2014 (and 2005) editions and were not re-checked against C651-23, so a change there is not confirmed.
new.title: Quick reference: water main test numbers
new.source: AWWA C600 (U.S. Pipe), utility specs, AWWA C651 summary

new.text: Key OSHA trench numbers (plain language; the regulation governs). Protective system required at 5 ft deep or more (unless stable rock), and in shallower trenches if a cave-in is possible. Over 20 ft the rule requires a system designed by a registered professional engineer, and OSHA's guidance treats 20 ft and deeper the same way, so plan on an engineer at 20 ft. Ladder or other exit required at 4 ft deep or more, within 25 ft of lateral travel. Spoil and equipment at least 2 ft from the edge. Atmosphere testing over 4 ft deep where hazardous atmosphere could exist: oxygen below 19.5% is deficient; flammable gas must stay below 20% of LFL. Maximum slopes: Type A 3/4 to 1; Type B 1 to 1; Type C 1-1/2 to 1. Shield: may dig up to 2 ft below the box only if rated for full depth with no soil loss. Daily inspection by the competent person, and after rain. State plans can be stricter; the job state's own rule governs.
new.title: Quick reference: trench safety numbers

old_title: Quick reference: locate color codes and tolerance zone

new.text: APWA locate colors: red electric; yellow gas, oil, steam; orange communications; blue potable water; purple reclaimed water and irrigation; green sewer and storm drain; white proposed excavation; pink temporary survey marks. Tolerance zone: set by each state's one-call law (18 or 24 inches each side of the marked facility in most laws); hand dig or vacuum excavate inside it. The notice time before digging and how long a ticket lasts are also set by the job state's one-call law, so check that state's rule. Locators don't mark depth. Check your state's one-call law.
new.title: Quick reference: locate color codes and tolerance zone
new.source: APWA uniform color code; state one-call laws

new.text: Joint deflection numbers to know (always check the maker for your joint). Ductile iron push-on (McWane chart, 18 ft lengths): 3 to 30 inch, 5 degrees, about 19 inches offset, about 205 ft radius; 36 inch, 4 degrees, about 15 inches, about 260 ft radius. DIPRA's guide (Table 5) lists 3 degrees for 14 inch and larger push-on joints: use 3 degrees unless you have the maker's chart. PVC: varies by maker; Westlake lists 1 degree for integral bell joints and 0.5 degree per side on their restrained coupling; solvent-weld joints none. Offset per degree (Uni-Bell): 4.2 inches on a 20 ft stick, 2.1 inches on 10 ft. Radius (ft) = 57.3 x length (ft) / degrees per joint. 1 degree vertical = about 1.75% slope change. Assemble joints straight and fully homed, then deflect. Gravity sewer is normally laid straight between manholes.
new.title: Quick reference: joint deflection

old_title: Quick reference: water and sewer separation

new.text: Ten States Standards separation (Recommended Standards for Water Works, 2018, 8.8): water mains at least 10 ft horizontally from gravity sanitary or storm sewers, edge to edge (8.8.2); crossings at least 18 inches outside to outside (8.8.3); anything less needs the reviewing authority's approval (8.8.4). Water over sewer at crossings. If the 10 ft or 18 inch can't be met: sewer built of water-main-grade pipe and pressure tested, or approved encasement; at crossings, water-grade sewer pipe 10 ft each side; if water goes under sewer, 18 inches clearance, support the sewer and center a full length of water pipe on the crossing. No water pipe through or touching a sewer manhole. The job state's own separation rule governs.
new.title: Quick reference: water and sewer separation
new.source: Recommended Standards for Water Works (Ten States Standards), 2018 edition, Sections 8.8.2-8.8.4 (our summary)

new.text: New mains are flushed before disinfection (except with the tablet method) to remove dirt, and after disinfection to remove heavily chlorinated water. AWWA C651-14 (Sec. 4.4.2) calls for flushing at 3.0 ft per second or more; the 2005 edition said about 2.5 ft per second, and specs written on it still say that. Flow needed for 3.0 ft per second (computed from pipe area): 4 inch about 120 gpm; 6 inch about 265 gpm; 8 inch about 470 gpm; 10 inch about 735 gpm; 12 inch about 1,060 gpm; 16 inch about 1,880 gpm (at 2.5 ft per second, 8 inch is about 390 gpm). Your spec or the water agency governs. A single 2-1/2 inch hydrant outlet may not deliver enough for larger mains, so use more outlets or the pumper nozzle. Flush until the water runs clear and, after disinfection, until the chlorine residual is no higher than the normal distribution system level. Control discharge to prevent erosion and dechlorinate per permit. Flow values are computed from area times velocity. AWWA lists C651-23 as the current edition of the disinfection standard; the numbers here are from the 2014 (and 2005) editions and were not re-checked against C651-23, so a change there is not confirmed.
new.title: Disinfection: flushing velocity and flow
new.topic: Testing: water main pressure test and disinfection
new.source: AWWA C651 summary, Open Exam Prep water operator study guide

old_title: Water main disinfection and bac-T samples (AWWA C651)

new.text: Keep pipe clean during laying, then disinfect before connecting to the system. AWWA C651 methods: continuous feed (water with at least 25 mg/L free chlorine fills the main, held 24 hours, ending with at least 10 mg/L), tablet (25 mg/L, 24 hours, water above 41 F), or slug (100 mg/L passed through for at least 3 hours). Agency specs can be stronger. Flush until the water is at system chlorine levels, dechlorinate the flush water before discharge, then take bacteriological (bac-T) samples: two sets that both pass, taken as the spec says (AWWA C651-14: a second set at least 16 hours after the first, or let the main sit 16 hours and take two sets 15 minutes apart; specs written on the 2005 edition say 24 hours apart), or per the agency; all must show no coliform. Don't connect until samples pass, and resample if the main isn't put in service in time. AWWA lists C651-23 as the current edition of the disinfection standard; the numbers here are from the 2014 (and 2005) editions and were not re-checked against C651-23, so a change there is not confirmed.
new.title: Water main disinfection and bac-T samples (AWWA C651)

old_title: How thrust works and how a block is sized

new.text: Water pressure pushes on every bend, tee, reducer, dead end and valve. Thrust on a bend T = 2 x P x A x sin(angle / 2); at a dead end or tee branch T = P x A; P = test pressure in psi (use the test pressure, not working), A = area of the pipe's outside diameter in square inches. Bearing area of the block = T x safety factor / allowable soil bearing (psf). Example: 8 in C900 (OD 9.05 in, A = 64.3 sq in) at 200 psi: a 90 degree bend pushes about 18,200 lb; a 45 about 9,850 lb; a dead end about 12,900 lb. In soil allowing 2,000 psf, the 90 needs about 9.1 sq ft of bearing face (before any safety factor). Soil bearing comes from the plans' thrust block detail or the geotech report; published tables disagree (sand is 2,000 psf in one DOT table and 4,000 in DIPRA's), so with no plan value ask the engineer and use the lower one.
new.title: How thrust works and how a block is sized
new.source: AWWA M41 (ductile iron) and M23 (PVC) thrust design; standard practice
